title: Triangles, the Pythagorean theorem and angles
blurb: Find a missing side of a right triangle, find missing angles in triangles and polygons, and use complementary, supplementary and vertical angles.
question: A 25 ft ladder leans against a clinic wall with its foot 7 ft from the base of the wall. How high up the wall does the ladder reach?

teach.body: Formally, in a right triangle with legs a and b and hypotenuse c, a² + b² = c². The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle (90°) and is always the longest side. In plain English: square the two shorter sides, add them, and you get the square of the longest side. It works ONLY for right triangles, and c must be the hypotenuse.

head: Legs a, b
Hypotenuse c
Check a² + b² = c²
teach.caption: Multiples of a triple are triples too: 6-8-10 and 9-12-15 are 3-4-5 times 2 and times 3. Spotting one saves calculator time.

items: Find the hypotenuse: the diagonal of a 9 ft × 12 ft rectangle. 9² + 12² = 81 + 144 = 225. c = √225 = 15 ft. Check: 15 × 15 = 225.
Find a leg: a 13 ft ladder with its foot 5 ft from a wall. The ladder is the hypotenuse. b² = 13² - 5² = 169 - 25 = 144. b = √144 = 12 ft up the wall. Check: 25 + 144 = 169.

teach.h: Find c first, then add or subtract
teach.body: Before calculating, label the hypotenuse: the side across from the right angle, such as the ladder, the diagonal or the straight-line distance. Finding the hypotenuse? ADD the squares, then take the square root. Finding a leg? SUBTRACT the smaller square from c², then take the square root. Never add the sides themselves (a + b is not c), and never stop at c² without the square root.

teach.caption: Angles all the way around a point add up to 360°.
Memory hook: C comes before S, and 90 comes before 180. When two lines cross, opposite angles are equal and side-by-side angles are supplementary.

children.label: Equilateral / isosceles / scalene
children.sub: 3 equal (60° each) / 2 equal, equal base angles / none equal

teach.caption: A triangle can never have two right angles or two obtuse angles: the sum would pass 180°.

teach.h: Angle sums in triangles and polygons
items: Triangle: the angles add to 180°. With 47° and 68°: 180 - 47 - 68 = 65°. Check: 47 + 68 + 65 = 180.
Isosceles triangle with a 40° vertex angle: the two base angles are equal, (180 - 40) ÷ 2 = 70° each.
Any polygon with n sides: angle sum = (n - 2) × 180°. Quadrilateral: 2 × 180 = 360°. Hexagon: 4 × 180 = 720°.
Regular polygon (all angles equal): divide the sum by n. Regular hexagon: 720 ÷ 6 = 120° each.

teach.body: Brianna, a nursing applicant helping with clinic maintenance, leans a 17 ft ladder against a wall with its foot 8 ft out. The ladder is the hypotenuse, so subtract: 17² - 8² = 289 - 64 = 225, and √225 = 15 ft up the wall (an 8-15-17 triple). The ladder meets the ground at 62°. The wall and ground form a 90° angle, so the angle at the top is 180 - 90 - 62 = 28°: the two acute angles of a right triangle are complementary.

teach.text: Pythagorean slips: adding the sides (a + b = c), forgetting the square root, and treating the hypotenuse as a leg (adding when you should subtract). Angle slips: mixing up complementary (90°) with supplementary (180°), and using 360° for a triangle.

items: Right triangles only: a² + b² = c², with c the hypotenuse (opposite the right angle, longest side).
Hypotenuse: add squares, square-root. Leg: subtract squares, square-root.
Complementary 90°; supplementary 180°; vertical angles equal; around a point 360°.

summary: You can now use a² + b² = c² to find either a hypotenuse or a leg, and recognize the common triples. You can also find missing angles in triangles and polygons and use complementary, supplementary and vertical angle relationships.

A.q: A right triangle has legs of 9 cm and 12 cm. What is the length of the hypotenuse, to the nearest tenth?

whyNot.1: This adds the legs (9 + 12); the squares must be added, not the sides.
whyNot.2: This stops at c² = 225 and forgets the square root.
whyNot.3: This treats 12 as the hypotenuse and subtracts: √(144 - 81).

A.q: An isosceles triangle has a vertex angle of 40°. What is the measure of each base angle?
A.why: The base angles are equal and all three angles total 180°: (180 - 40) ÷ 2 = 70° each. Check: 40 + 70 + 70 = 180.

whyNot.0: 140° is the two base angles together; it must be split equally.
whyNot.1: This assumes all three angles are equal, which would make it equilateral (60° each).
whyNot.3: This uses 360°, the sum for a quadrilateral: (360 - 40) ÷ 2.

A.q: Angles A and B are complementary. Angle A measures 34°. What is the measure of angle B?

whyNot.0: This uses 180°, which is for supplementary angles.
whyNot.2: This treats the angles as equal, which is true of vertical angles.
whyNot.3: This uses 360°, the total around a point.

B.q: A 25 ft ladder leans against a wall with its foot 7 ft from the base of the wall. How high up the wall does the ladder reach, to the nearest tenth?
B.why: The ladder is the hypotenuse. b² = 25² - 7² = 625 - 49 = 576, so b = √576 = 24.0 ft. Check: 49 + 576 = 625.

whyNot.0: This adds the squares (√674), treating the ladder as a leg instead of the hypotenuse.
whyNot.1: This subtracts the lengths themselves (25 - 7) instead of their squares.

B.q: What is the measure of each interior angle of a regular hexagon?
B.why: Angle sum = (6 - 2) × 180 = 720°. A regular hexagon has 6 equal angles: 720 ÷ 6 = 120°.

whyNot.1: This divides 360° by 6, which gives the angle at the center, not an interior angle.
whyNot.2: 720° is the sum of all six interior angles, not each one.
whyNot.3: This uses n × 180 = 1,080° instead of (n - 2) × 180 before dividing by 6.

B.q: Two straight lines cross, forming four angles. One of the angles measures 72°. What are the other three, going around the crossing?
B.why: Side-by-side angles along a straight line are supplementary: 180 - 72 = 108°. The opposite (vertical) angle equals 72°. Check: 72 + 108 + 72 + 108 = 360.

whyNot.0: Only the opposite (vertical) angle equals 72°; the neighbors must make a straight line with it.
whyNot.1: This uses complementary angles (90 - 72); neighbors on a straight line sum to 180°.
whyNot.3: The angle opposite the 72° angle is vertical to it, so it is also 72°.

C.q: A rectangular TV screen is 32 in wide and 24 in tall. What is the length of its diagonal, to the nearest whole inch?
C.why: The diagonal is the hypotenuse: 32² + 24² = 1,024 + 576 = 1,600, and √1,600 = 40 in. (It is 3-4-5 times 8.)

whyNot.0: This adds the width and height instead of their squares.
whyNot.2: This subtracts the squares (√448), treating the width as the hypotenuse.
whyNot.3: This stops at c² and forgets the square root.

C.q: In triangle ABC, angle B is 3 times angle A, and angle C is 20° more than angle A. What is the measure of angle C?

whyNot.0: 32° is angle A, an intermediate answer; angle C is 20° more.
whyNot.1: 96° is angle B (3 × 32), not angle C.
whyNot.2: This leaves the A out of angle C (A + 3A + 20 = 180 gives A = 40), then adds 20.

C.q: Which set of side lengths forms a right triangle?
C.why: Test a² + b² = c² with the longest side as c: 25 + 144 = 169 = 13². None of the other sets works.

whyNot.0: 16 + 25 = 41, but 6² = 36, so it is not a right triangle.
whyNot.3: 7 + 8 = 15 adds the sides, not their squares: 49 + 64 = 113, not 225.

reteach.title: Think of a shortcut across a parking lot
reteach.question: You can walk along two edges of a rectangular parking lot or cut straight across it. How does that explain the Pythagorean theorem?

blocks.body: Walking along two edges of a lot 60 m by 80 m covers 140 m. Cutting straight across the diagonal is shorter: 60² + 80² = 3,600 + 6,400 = 10,000, and √10,000 = 100 m. The two edges are the legs and the shortcut is the hypotenuse. It is always longer than either leg but shorter than the two legs added, which is a quick way to sense-check any answer.

blocks.h: Three routes in a 60 m × 80 m lot
blocks.caption: The hypotenuse (100 m) lies between the longest leg (80 m) and the sum of the legs (140 m).

blocks.text: If your hypotenuse equals a + b, you added sides instead of squares. If it is shorter than a leg, you subtracted when you should have added.

explain.body: Square both legs, add, then take the square root. Diagonals of rectangles and straight-line distances are hypotenuses.

test.q: A rectangular park is 80 m long and 60 m wide. How long is a straight path along its diagonal, to the nearest whole meter?

whyNot.0: This adds the lengths instead of their squares.
whyNot.1: This subtracts the squares (√2,800), treating a side as the hypotenuse.
whyNot.2: This stops at c² without the square root.

explain.body: When the hypotenuse is known, subtract: b² = c² - a², then take the square root.

test.q: A right triangle has a hypotenuse of 17 in and one leg of 8 in. What is the length of the other leg, to the nearest whole inch?

whyNot.0: This adds the squares (√353), treating 17 as a leg.
whyNot.2: This subtracts the lengths (17 - 8), not their squares.

explain.body: The three angles of any triangle add up to 180°. Find the missing angle by subtracting, then classify: one angle of exactly 90° makes a right triangle.

test.q: Two angles of a triangle measure 35° and 55°. How is the triangle classified by its angles?
test.why: The third angle is 180 - 35 - 55 = 90°, so it is a right triangle.

whyNot.1: The two given angles are acute, but the third is 90°, so not all three are less than 90°.
whyNot.3: An equilateral triangle has three 60° angles.

explain.body: Complementary angles sum to 90°, supplementary to 180°, and vertical angles are equal. Set up an equation when one angle is described in terms of the other.

test.q: Angles P and Q are supplementary, and angle P is 4 times angle Q. What is the measure of angle P?

whyNot.0: 36° is angle Q, an intermediate answer.
whyNot.3: This splits 180° into 4 parts instead of 5 (4 parts for P plus 1 for Q), giving Q = 45° and P = 135°.
